summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The prompt_contract phase concluded with full agreement on both process and substance. Scope: a single native SwiftUI iOS app with a real, deployed, reachable backend — no multi-app hedging, no offline-only version, and no reskinned todo/habit/journal/AI-wrapper core. The working concept is a real-time care-and-handoff relay network for parents/guardians of children under 13 needing same-day pickup/handoff support, carried forward provisionally (not immutably locked) and subject to rollback if it fails a live two-device/two-account load-bearing backend test. A critical safety constraint was added after Claude flagged that open proximity-based stranger matching for child handoffs is a real liability, not an edge case: matching must be restricted to a pre-established trust graph (contacts, or verified members of a school/daycare pod a parent explicitly joins), and no UI may imply identity verification or background-check vetting that wasn't actually performed — self-reported/peer-vouched trust must be labeled honestly. Consent artifacts, verifier IDs, and audit/event logs are first-class data model objects. Production-readiness is defined by checkable behavior: real empty/loading/error/success states verified via airplane mode and fresh-account testing, auth persistence across force-quit, and no UI claiming Saved/Synced/Sent/Accepted without genuine backend acknowledgment. Both participants agreed the architecture phase's first deliverable must be proof that a real backend endpoint is deployed and reachable from the iOS client, before any concept-specific schema or screens are trusted. Naming and pitch framing must lead with the trust-graph/pod mechanic rather than generic 'matching' to avoid reading as derivative or alarming. A full 18-item numbered testable requirements list was produced covering platform, backend reachability, load-bearing multi-user behavior, trust-graph-restricted matching, anti-fake-vetting UI rules, state handling, onboarding, persistence, visual design tokens/dark mode, and pre-build API/data-model/sync documentation.
open_risks: The relay concept still carries residual child-safety sensitivity even with trust-graph-only matching — later phases must not quietly relax that constraint under build-time pressure

Backend reachability from this build environment is asserted as a requirement but not yet actually proven — the architecture phase must deliver this proof early or the whole 'requires a backend' premise is unverified
Trust-graph/pod onboarding (joining a school/daycare pod, vouching flow) adds real UX complexity that must not be dropped for a simpler-but-unsafe proximity-matching shortcut under time pressure

The 'stranger would say that's clever' bar remains partly subjective; the hard-to-fake and non-saturated-clone tie-breakers exist but still require a later phase to apply them concretely to the naming/pitch

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The product_research phase concluded with the concept reframed as a 'micro-supply network for immediate care continuity' — coordinating a temporary trust transfer among people who already know each other (a specific school pickup pod), not a marketplace or matching app. The real incumbent identified is the plain class WhatsApp/GroupMe thread, whose gaps (no live acceptance state, no de-duplication of simultaneous 'I got it' replies, no accountability record) justify the backend requirement. Comparable patterns (Life360, ClassDojo/Brightwheel, Nextdoor, HopSkipDrive, Uber/Lyft) were named as ASSUMPTIONs to calibrate what to avoid: map-centric design, open-board social-discovery feel, and paid/background-checked trust models rejected in the prior phase. The team locked a narrow first-build scope: exactly one pod type (school pickup only, no daycare/activity in v1), no GPS/live location, no child PII (names/photos), and an invite-link or admin-issued pod-join-code flow with a real empty state so onboarding doesn't dead-end for users without an existing pod. The accept-flow race condition was elevated to a named, testable first-build acceptance criterion: server-side first-accept-wins via conditional/compare-and-swap update, an explicit 'already claimed' state for the losing acceptor, sub-30-second propagation target, and a required two-device concurrent-accept test case. The audit/evidence log and the shareable 'relay receipt' viral artifact were merged into a single underlying data object with two views — an internal audit record and a privacy-filtered shareable summary card — satisfying both the safety/audit requirement and the growth mechanic with one data model decision. Cold-start/network-density risk was acknowledged as unprovable within this build cycle; the agreed mitigation is minimizing marginal join friction and requiring a second real seeded pod-member account as a first-class part of the app's own verification protocol going forward.
open_risks: Notification/APNs delivery latency needs to hit sub-minute practical responsiveness for the pain point to be meaningfully addressed, and this is unverified in this build environment
Legal/privacy requirements around any child-related data and real-world tolerance for consent/audit artifacts in actual households remain unknowns not resolvable by design alone
The single-pod-type, no-location, no-PII scope cuts are locked for v1 but must not quietly erode under build-time pressure to add 'just one more' pod type or convenience feature
Cold-start/network-density at realistic pod scale (15-20 families) remains genuinely unproven and can only be partially mitigated, not solved, by low-friction onboarding

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The portfolio_selection phase confirmed, with no disagreement, that this build is a single native iOS app with no portfolio split — consistent with the singular-app framing locked in prompt_contract and the inherently non-decomposable relay mechanic from product_research. The selected app is slug pulse-relay, framed as real-time trust-graph coordination/social-utility (not marketplace, not generic matching), with the promise that a parent's pod knows within seconds when pickup coverage is needed and exactly one person locks in acceptance with no double coverage. The target user is a parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a specific, pre-existing school-pickup pod facing an unplanned same-day pickup conflict. Rejected alternatives include any sibling-app split (separate requester/helper apps, a pod-admin companion app), generic banned-category reskins, single-user-only designs, open stranger matching, daycare/activity pod variants, and location-tracking-first designs — none of which fit the locked single-app, single-pod-type scope. A build-priority decision was added: if time is constrained, cuts should come from secondary screens (pod management, profile/settings) rather than from the fidelity or correctness of the two core funnels (post relay request, accept/conflict-resolve/complete) or the accept race-condition test, since the core loop's trustworthiness is the entire value proposition and cannot be recovered by any secondary feature once broken.
open_risks: No new risks introduced this phase; all risks carried forward from prompt_contract and product_research (backend reachability unproven until architecture phase, cold-start/network-density unprovable in this build cycle, race-condition arbitration must be a real server-side mechanism and not just a demo-passing illusion) remain open and must be addressed in upcoming phases.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The initial_discussion phase locked a single, mutually-confirmed product definition for pulse-relay across two rounds. Product promise: a parent in a school-pickup pod broadcasts a same-day pickup coverage need and exactly one trusted pod member locks it in via a server-arbitrated first-accept-wins mechanism, with no ambiguity and no silent failure states. Primary user: a parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a specific, pre-existing school-pickup pod, acting one-handed under real time pressure with roughly ninety seconds of attention. The core loop was locked with explicit named states end-to-end: post request (no child PII) -> live pod visibility + push deep-link -> accept -> server-arbitrated first-accept-wins -> confirmed/already-covered states -> optional release/reopen -> optional time-aware still-open escalation with re-broadcast -> complete -> combined audit/receipt record. Two failure-mode requirements were elevated to core-loop, non-secondary status: acceptance is reversible until handoff completion, with an explicit release action that reopens the request and re-notifies the pod (~30s target), because an unretractable 'confirmed' state manufactures dangerous false certainty; and an unfulfilled request must show a visible, time-aware 'still open' state (not silence or a static pending label), because silent ambiguity on an actually-open request is an equally dangerous failure mode. The data model was required to support multiple simultaneously-open requests per pod (not a single-active-request assumption), even if the UI leads with a focused single card. The pod-creator role was locked as deliberately minimal (create pod, get join code/link, nothing more) consistent with the earlier build-priority rule to cut secondary screens first. A tier of hard, non-negotiable scope boundaries was finalized at the same priority level as the pre-existing location/child-PII bans: no in-app chat/DM thread (request card plus one optional short note only), no recurring/scheduled requests (same-day only), no payments, and no persistent scrollable request-history feed beyond the per-request audit/receipt artifact. Measurable success criteria were finalized covering backend reachability proof, zero-dead-end pod join/create, four-state screens, the two-device concurrent-accept race test, sub-minute notification delivery, sub-30-second release/reopen re-notification, time-aware unfulfilled escalation, force-quit session/state persistence, and a required two-real-seeded-account verification protocol.
open_risks: The multi-concurrent-open-request data model requirement adds real complexity to the API contract and UI ordering/disambiguation logic that the next phase must actually design, not hand-wave

The release/reopen and still-open escalation flows are new core-loop requirements that add build surface area beyond the original two-funnel framing and must not be quietly descoped under time pressure given portfolio_selection's build-priority rule

All risks carried forward from prompt_contract, product_research, and portfolio_selection remain open (backend reachability unproven, cold-start/network-density unprovable in this build cycle, race-condition arbitration must be genuinely server-side and pass a real concurrent test, not just look correct in a demo)

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The per_app_product_brief phase closed with full agreement across two rounds on a production-grade brief for pulse-relay. Target user: a parent/guardian in one specific, named school-pickup pod, a rare/emergency-use app rather than a daily-engagement product, whose real pain is the ambiguity of a group chat where multiple people claim coverage at once or nobody claims it. The core loop was restated unchanged from initial_discussion (post request, no child PII -> live pod visibility + deep-linked push -> server-arbitrated first-accept-wins -> explicit claimed/already-covered/reopened/still-open/error states -> completion produces one combined audit/receipt object). Subscription value was locked to exactly three unlocks -- multi-pod membership, exportable/signed receipt-and-audit history for custody/co-parenting documentation, and critical-alert-tier notifications that bypass Focus/DND -- with response-time analytics and escalation-policy customization explicitly deferred out of v1 after Claude showed they either don't survive contact with existing free-tier safety requirements or lack a validated paying user. A new hard rule was locked: the free tier includes every core relay action and the full state machine forever for at least one pod, with nothing safety-related ever gated behind payment. The growth/viral mechanic was locked as an explicit, unglamorous reliability requirement -- the core loop must work flawlessly on every new pod's first real incident -- with the shareable receipt card demoted to a secondary proof artifact that supports word-of-mouth but is not itself the growth lever, and an explicit warning against building an 'invite your pod' referral screen as if it were the growth feature. Local-first behavior was finalized with a hard no-optimistic-confirmation rule: reads render instantly from cache, but any outcome-affecting write (accept/release/complete) must show an explicit awaiting-confirmation state and never a premature success flash before real server acknowledgment. Cloud-ready extensions beyond v1 (pod-type-as-config, multi-guardian household identity, pod-health analytics) were named but explicitly deferred, not built now.
open_risks: The three-unlock subscription model is untested against real willingness-to-pay and may need revisiting once usage data exists, but is locked for v1 planning purposes

The 'flawless first incident per pod' growth requirement places significant pressure on notification latency and race-condition correctness being right on the very first real use, with no room for a soft launch or gradual rollout per pod

All risks carried forward from prompt_contract, product_research, portfolio_selection, and initial_discussion remain open (backend reachability unproven, cold-start/network-density unprovable in this build cycle, race-condition arbitration must be genuinely server-side and pass a real concurrent test, not just look correct in a demo)

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The next_steps_small phase locked the MVP slice for pulse-relay across two rounds with full agreement. The slice is defined as the entire core loop end-to-end, not a stripped-down subset: fresh account bootstrap, join/create pod by invite code with no dead-end, post a same-day request with no child PII, live visibility plus a real APNs-delivered deep-linked push to a second seeded account, a two-account concurrent accept-race resolved by a genuine server-side compare-and-swap write into exactly one confirmed winner and one explicit 'already covered by [name]' loser (both gated on backend acknowledgment, never optimistic), an accepter release that reopens and re-notifies the pod within ~30 seconds, a visibly time-aware 'still open' state with re-broadcast for unaccepted requests, and completion producing one combined audit/receipt object visible to both parties. Both participants independently converged on the same must-have interactions (explicit awaiting-confirmation states on every outcome-affecting action, real four-state screens on both funnels, elapsed-time labeling, force-quit persistence) and the same cut list (no subscription/paywall, no multi-pod, no receipt export, no critical-alert tier, no pod-admin beyond create-pod-get-code, no chat/DM, no recurring/scheduled requests, no payments, no analytics, no history/feed, no polish-only visual work). Two points Claude raised in round 1 were explicitly confirmed and locked by Codex in round 2: the accept-race 'already covered' loser transition is critical-path, non-negotiable-quality UX carved out of the polish-cut bucket and prioritized above other visual work including the receipt card; and this slice is explicitly barred from using polling or client-side arbitration as a stand-in for real server-side CAS and real APNs push delivery, even though such a stand-in could pass the same UI-state checklist, because it would leave the backend's load-bearing status and the prompt's 'server-driven push notifications' justification unproven. A fourth point, introduced by Claude in round 2 without an explicit prior round of cross-confirmation but not contradicted by anything Codex said, was folded in as the phase's overarching acceptance bar: a literal two-phone side-by-side demo (one device shows confirmed, the other shows already-covered-by-name, within a second or two, zero chat, zero manual reconciliation) is the real test this slice is judged against, with all the itemized validation criteria serving as its constituent parts rather than a separate flat checklist.
open_risks: The APNs + server-side CAS requirement raises real build complexity and risk in this build environment compared to a simpler polling-based fake, and must not be quietly softened once build work actually starts under time pressure
The 'already covered' transition's design-priority status depends on the next design phase actually naming and treating it specially rather than defaulting to generic error-state styling

The two-phone demo as acceptance bar requires two genuinely separate devices/accounts to run, which must be treated as a required step, not an optional nice-to-have, consistent with DEC-product_research-008

All risks carried forward from every prior phase remain open (backend reachability unproven until actually tested, cold-start/network-density unprovable in this build cycle, race-condition arbitration must be genuinely server-side and pass a real concurrent test under real timing, not just look correct in a demo)

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The detailed_discussion phase closed after three rounds with ten locked decisions that resolve the concrete edge cases threatening the pulse-relay core loop's 'no ambiguity, ever' promise, without expanding scope. Notification honesty: the app shows literal delivery-count copy ('Sent to N pod members') based on real push-token status rather than implying full visibility, an accepted free-tier limitation given no critical-alert/DND-bypass on free accounts. Time handling: same-day cutoffs and elapsed/aging math are computed server-side in UTC against a pod-home-timezone set at pod creation, with no client-local-time logic. Idempotency: every outcome-affecting action (post/accept/release/complete/withdraw) uses client-generated action IDs handled idempotently server-side, with relaunch-after-crash reconciling from server truth, and a named force-quit-mid-accept test joins the two-phone race demo as an acceptance check. Join-code security: the pod-creator gains exactly one new capability, revoke-and-reissue, as a narrow escape hatch for a leaked or misdirected code, without reopening the cut admin-console surface. A brand-new, member-less pod gets a distinct empty state/CTA separate from an unresponsive-but-populated pod. The audit/receipt record survives either party's account deletion, rendering the departed party as a placeholder so neither side can unilaterally erase shared documentation. UI copy must state explicitly that 'accepted' means only claimed responsibility, not guaranteed arrival. The phase's central late-breaking decision: a new first-class, requester-only `withdrawn` terminal state was added for open/unclaimed requests, arbitrated through the same server-side CAS path as accept, producing a real push re-notify but never an audit/receipt artifact, and visually/semantically distinct from `complete` -- added specifically to prevent a self-resolved situation from leaving a stale, escalating request that a good-faith pod member could act on unnecessarily. This was reconciled with the original no-cancel safety concern by making `withdrawn` and `release` mutually exclusive by state (only one is ever visible to a given user at a given time), eliminating the ambiguity risk that motivated the original hesitation. Finally, v1's lack of any moderation/reporting/removal capability for bad-faith posting was named and accepted as an explicit, documented v1 limitation rather than something to build now, mitigated only by trust-graph invite-only membership, per-request attribution, and the new code-revocation capability.
open_risks: The new `withdrawn` state adds a third CAS-arbitrated outcome (alongside accept/already-covered) that the architecture phase must design and test with the same rigor as the accept race, including its interaction with in-flight accepts
Free-tier notification reliability remains a named, unsolved risk to the 'flawless first incident' growth requirement -- it is documented honestly, not fixed
The accepted v1 spam/bad-faith-posting limitation could become a real problem at scale and has no built-in escalation trigger for when to revisit it

All risks carried forward from every prior phase remain open (backend reachability unproven until actually tested, cold-start/network-density unprovable in this build cycle, race-condition arbitration must be genuinely server-side and pass a real concurrent test under real timing)

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The app_features phase closed after three rounds with a fully cross-confirmed MoSCoW breakdown and a 39-item numbered requirements contract for pulse-relay's v1 build. The must-have set is the entire MVP slice locked in next_steps_small/detailed_discussion, organized into execution-priority tiers for scheduling purposes only (never for correctness erosion): Tier-1 is the literal two-phone demo spine (auth persistence, zero-dead-end pod onboarding, no-PII posting with awaiting-confirmation, honest delivery-count copy, a bounded server-side CAS-commit-plus-APNs-dispatch contract, and deterministic CAS-based accept-race arbitration yielding one confirmed winner and one explicit already-covered-by-name loser), while Tier-2 (release/reopen, the withdrawn terminal state mutually exclusive with release, still-open aging with re-broadcast, and completion producing the dual-view audit/receipt) remains fully required but may absorb reduced visual finish first under time pressure. Six requirements (honest delivery copy, server-side CAS, deterministic winner/loser, non-optimistic terminal confirmation, the bounded push-dispatch commitment, and the two-device demo itself) are explicitly flagged demo-critical/uncuttable within the requirements document, removing any inference burden from a build agent under deadline pressure. The APNs push requirement was refined into an honest two-part contract: the backend must commit the CAS write and submit the push payload within a strict server-owned bound (~2s target), while actual device receipt timing is observed in the two-device demo empirically but is not a hard contractual pass/fail metric, since Apple's push infrastructure is best-effort. The tokenized Theme.swift system and full light/dark coverage on every core screen was elevated from a 'should' to a hard must-have with explicit design-lint parity (no style literals outside the theme file, both appearances verified), directly citing this fleet's own two prior recorded design-lint incidents (hardcoded font size, hardcoded inline color) as the reason it cannot be left as optional polish. Subscription-tier features (multi-pod, receipt export, critical-alert bypass) were locked as explicitly out of implementation scope for this build — no StoreKit, no paywall UI, no gated core behavior, at most an inert unused entitlement field. The full pre-existing won't-build list (child PII, location/GPS/ETA, chat/DM, payments, recurring/scheduled requests, history feed, admin console beyond code rotation, moderation, fake-vetting badges, stranger matching) was reaffirmed unchanged. The phase produced a complete, numbered, testable requirements-json contract (R-001 through R-039) that the adherence gate will grade the built app against, and a should/could list (deterministic request ordering, retry/backoff copy, subtle transition haptics, onboarding helper card, minimal profile/sign-out screen, receipt-card visual polish subordinate to the already-covered transition, inert entitlement schema field) explicitly scoped as secondary to the locked must-haves.
open_risks: The demo-critical/uncuttable tagging depends on later architecture and build phases actually carrying it forward verbatim rather than treating it as this phase's internal bookkeeping
The theme/dark-mode hard-must status must be reflected consistently in the design phase's own artifacts, not just this phase's documents, or the same should/must drift could recur
The bounded server-side push-dispatch target (~2s) is asserted here but not yet measured against this build environment's real APNs integration path

All risks carried forward from every prior phase remain open (backend reachability unproven until actually tested, cold-start/network-density unprovable in this build cycle, race-condition arbitration must be genuinely server-side and pass a real concurrent test under real timing)

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The design_discussion phase closed after three rounds with a fully cross-confirmed visual identity for pulse-relay, locked as 'Relay HUD.' The design language is an instrument-panel identity meant to read as trustworthy under stress rather than alarming: status-bearing cards (never default List/Form/system-blue chrome, never toast confirmations) driven entirely by one Theme.swift file, using a semantic palette of amber-pulse (open/awaiting), warm teal-green (confirmed/claimed), slate/muted gray (withdrawn/complete terminal states), with true red reserved exclusively for genuine system errors and explicitly barred from ever rendering the accept-race loser state. The signature interaction is a pulse-to-latch motion — cards pulse on a calm heartbeat while awaiting server acknowledgment, then convert to a steady locked panel on resolution — applied identically to both the accept-race winner ('claimed/confirmed') and loser ('already covered by [name]'), with no shake/alert-icon/red treatment on the loser, so the demo-critical losing transition visually reads as 'worked as designed' rather than a malfunction; this motion is embodied in code as a component informally called BeaconCard/RelayBeaconView, with 'Beacon' surviving only as that component name, not as part of the product's design-language name. Screen scope stays deliberately narrow (session/auth, pod onboarding with true empty states, live relay board, request composer, request detail for accept/release/withdraw, receipt, minimal profile/pod-settings) with no added branching. Secondary screens (receipt, profile, pod settings) inherit Theme tokens but are explicitly barred from custom transitions, bespoke empty-state illustration, and any color treatment outside the shared semantic palette, with a narrow carve-out that the receipt card gets a higher typography/information-hierarchy bar (since it leaves the app via share sheet) but still no unique animation. A late but uncontested addition locked the live board's default 'all clear' resting state — the screen seen the vast majority of the time given this app's rare-but-critical usage pattern — as a real composed screen (pod name, member count, an at-rest slate/teal 'all clear' indicator, and the post-request CTA), not a blank placeholder, consistent with the pre-existing global rule that empty states are designed content. Finally, an explicit craft-budget priority order was locked for time pressure: the open-to-awaiting pulse, then the deterministic winner/loser latch, then completed/withdrawn terminal clarity, with everything else built plain rather than polished if time runs short.
open_risks: The pulse-to-latch motion's fidelity, especially the loser-state 'no error read' requirement, depends entirely on actual SwiftUI animation implementation quality in the build phase — this phase specifies intent precisely but cannot guarantee execution
The 'zero unique craft on secondary screens' constraint requires discipline during build under time pressure and has no automatic enforcement mechanism beyond this being written down

All risks carried forward from every prior phase remain open: backend reachability is unproven until actually tested, cold-start/network-density is unprovable in this build cycle, and the CAS/APNs race-arbitration path must be genuinely server-side and pass a real concurrent two-device test, not just look correct visually

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The design_handoff phase closed after three rounds with a complete, buildable Relay HUD design spec for pulse-relay covering every required heading. The final token set: a 9-role type scale mapped to Dynamic Type, a 4pt spacing grid (4 through 40 plus named component metrics), a warm-neutral semantic color palette (correcting an earlier cool-blue draft that had quietly reintroduced the 'sci-fi HUD' register explicitly rejected in design_discussion) paired with the previously-locked state accents (amber pulse, warm teal confirmed, slate terminal, red reserved strictly for system errors), and six named corner radii. The component inventory (BeaconCard, PodHeaderBar, ConnectionBanner/SyncingBanner, RequestComposerSheet, RequestDetailSheet, DeepLinkStateView, ReceiptCard, etc.) and navigation map (AppGate -> AuthGate/PodOnboarding/RelayBoard root, sheet-presented composer/detail, stack-pushed Profile/PodSettings, no tabs) are locked with no added branching. The request card state machine is fully specified with eleven named states including a hard split between awaitingConfirmation (own action in flight), queuedOffline (action stored locally, not yet sent), and reconciling (state learned via a push-triggered refetch after another device's action) -- collapsing any of these was identified as the most likely way a build agent would silently break the two-device demo. A non-negotiable architectural rule was written explicitly: push notification payloads are never rendered as state; every push is a wake-up signal that triggers an authoritative refetch, and the UI transitions only after that fetch resolves. Board ordering is locked as server-authoritative displayOrder (created-at ascending plus tie-break) with no client-side urgency concept, since no urgency field exists in the data model. Additional edge-case behavior was locked: a single top-level (not per-card) 'Syncing latest pod state...' banner covers cold-launch and force-quit-mid-action freshness, elapsed timers read MM:SS under an hour then 'Xh Ym', and the connection banner carries two distinct copy states for offline-queued versus uncertain-delivery rather than one vague message. Motion and haptics are fully specified (0.9s breathing pulse, 0.45s spring latch identical for accept-race winner and loser, ~0.15s Reduce Motion crossfade, non-judgmental haptics with no warning/error cue for the loser), alongside full per-screen loading/empty/error/success states with copy, icon, and recovery actions for all eight screens. Accessibility requirements (VoiceOver sentence-composition per card, 44x44 targets, AA contrast, Dynamic Type reflow at AX3-AX5, no color-only signaling) and the craft-budget priority order (pulse, then latch, then terminal clarity) are locked. The phase closed with an explicit decision to use no external Claude Design pass for this build -- implementation goes straight from this spec into SwiftUI, with the drafted upload prompt kept only as a future static-asset fallback.
open_risks: The pulse-to-latch motion's fidelity, especially the 'no error read' requirement on the accept-race loser, depends entirely on actual SwiftUI implementation quality and has not been built or tested yet

The push-payload-never-trusted architectural rule is now explicit in the spec but its correct implementation (gating every terminal transition on a real fetch, never on notification userInfo) is unverified until build and the two-device demo actually run
The 'zero unique craft on secondary screens' and craft-budget-priority constraints require build-time discipline under deadline pressure with no automatic enforcement beyond being written down

All risks carried forward from every prior phase remain open: backend reachability is unproven until actually tested, cold-start/network-density is unprovable in this build cycle, and CAS/APNs race-arbitration correctness must be demonstrated live, not just specified correctly on paper

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The ios_architecture_review phase closed after two rounds with a fully confirmed iOS architecture for pulse-relay. The backend is a custom REST API (/api/v1) over PostgreSQL, chosen specifically for compare-and-swap-safe transitions (first-accept-wins, mutually exclusive release/withdraw) and transactional audit/receipt logging; every outcome-affecting endpoint takes an idempotent client action ID and returns either the updated row or an explicit conflict payload. The client is architected around a single @Observable AppSession driving AppGate's three-way routing, with an actor-based RequestSyncCoordinator as the sole mutator of request state -- serializing the two concurrent producers (local user actions and push-triggered refetches) so illegal combined states are structurally impossible -- and card state modeled as a single Swift enum driven through a pure reducer, never booleans. Apple-first-party frameworks only: URLSession+async/await, Codable, SwiftData (disposable cache for board/request/receipt snapshots, purge-and-refetch on schema mismatch, no custom migration plan, but a durable outbox for queued offline actions that must survive relaunch/upgrade without silent loss), Keychain (session tokens with kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly so a locked-phone push can still authenticate a background refetch), AuthenticationServices, UserNotifications/APNs, and OSLog -- zero third-party dependencies, satisfying the permissive-license policy by not needing an exception. Permissions are minimal (Sign in with Apple, remote notifications only), with notification authorization requested after pod onboarding (not cold launch) with a rationale line, notification action buttons banned entirely in favor of deep-link-only interaction, and the primary reconciliation trigger defined as visible-alert-push-plus-tap-or-scenePhase-refetch rather than relying on throttleable silent content-available push. Critical Alerts stays unimplemented in v1 and is explicitly flagged as feasibility-uncertain for this app category, not assumed obtainable. Testing requires two independent acceptance tiers: a backend-only concurrent integration test (two simultaneous accept calls must yield exactly one success and one deterministic conflict, plus an accept-vs-withdraw race test) proving the CAS mechanism, run alongside (not instead of) the manual two-phone demo proving the experience.
open_risks: The actor-based coordinator and enum state machine are specified but not yet implemented or tested against real concurrent push/local-action timing
The Keychain accessibility choice and durable-outbox-across-upgrade behavior need to be verified with actual locked-device and app-version-upgrade test scenarios during build, not just specified
The backend concurrent integration test is now a required acceptance gate but has not yet been written or run against a real implementation

All risks carried forward from every prior phase remain open: backend reachability is unproven until actually tested, cold-start/network-density is unprovable in this build cycle, and CAS/APNs race-arbitration correctness must be demonstrated live, not just specified correctly on paper

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The tech_specs phase closed after three rounds with a fully reconciled, buildable architecture and data contract for pulse-relay, built on the ios_architecture_review skeleton (server-authoritative REST/PostgreSQL, actor-based RequestSyncCoordinator, AppSession, SwiftData disposable cache plus durable outbox, Keychain, zero third-party dependencies). The canonical domain model uses a plain 'Request'-family naming convention (Request, RequestStatus, RequestAction, ActionType, ActionResult, Receipt, Pod, PodMembership, User) after both participants swapped naming preferences mid-round-2 and then explicitly reconciled in round 3. Expired-vs-withdrawn requests are represented by keeping RequestStatus at exactly 5 values plus a separate closeReason field (autoExpired/requesterWithdrawn/systemHousekeeping), preserving the locked 11-state client card machine from design_handoff without adding a 12th state. ActionType includes a required reBroadcast case per the locked re-broadcast requirement. Every outcome-affecting action write requires a non-optional expectedRequestRevision parameter threaded from the offline outbox through the coordinator to the wire endpoint, enforced via a Postgres compare-and-swap UPDATE that returns either the updated row or an explicit conflict payload; RequestAction is a standalone, always-written audit-log table never owned by the Receipt object, since withdrawn/expired requests never produce a receipt but still need a queryable trail. A required GET /api/v1/health endpoint gates client trust in any backend-dependent state on reachability and contract version. A hard server-side single-pod-per-account cap (403 already_in_pod) is locked for v1 given multi-pod is entitlement-gated and out of scope. Board ordering uses a single BIGSERIAL-backed displayOrder column with no client re-sort. A third mandatory verification tier was added beyond the previously locked backend concurrency test and manual two-phone demo: a local coordinator-concurrency test racing two real RequestSyncCoordinator instances against one shared test backend via TaskGroup, asserting the winner/loser split lands correctly in each actor's own event stream. The Red Team's required contribution for this phase was a new edge case: queued offline actions that come back with a real conflict/forbidden/unauthorized outcome must be treated as terminal and stop retrying, with only network/timeout failures retriable, preventing a definitively-rejected action from leaving the UI in false-confidence limbo. Two purely cosmetic leftover naming inconsistencies (RequestAPIClient vs PulseRelayAPIClient, AppError vs RelayError) were resolved directly by the coordinator as a tie-break rather than spending a fourth round on them. Module layout (App/Domain/State/Network/Persistence/Notifications/Features/Shared) and the full API/data-model contract are locked and ready for parallel build-lane implementation.
open_risks: The new local coordinator-concurrency test tier is specified but not yet implemented or run against real actor/network timing

The terminal-vs-retriable conflict classification for queued offline actions is a new requirement that must be explicitly covered by reducer unit tests during build, not assumed correct from the spec alone
The closeReason mechanism for expired-vs-withdrawn has not been exercised against a real same-day expiry scheduled job or lazy check-on-read implementation yet

All risks carried forward from every prior phase remain open: backend reachability is unproven until actually tested, cold-start/network-density is unprovable in this build cycle, and CAS/APNs race-arbitration correctness must be demonstrated live across all three verification tiers, not just specified correctly on paper

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The project_plan phase closed after two rounds with a fully reconciled nine-milestone delivery plan for pulse-relay. Milestone 0 pins the previously-unstated backend implementation choice: Node.js + TypeScript, a thin HTTP layer, node-postgres against managed Postgres, deployed to a real public HTTPS host already available in this workspace, with an explicit, testable exit criterion — an external, non-localhost curl of /api/v1/health returning canOperate:true — replacing the prior phases' unproven 'custom REST over PostgreSQL' architecture-only framing. The locked two-phone real-APNs demo acceptance bar from next_steps_small is preserved as the ideal target but explicitly tiered: run for real if a paid Apple Developer account, push-capable provisioning, and two physical devices are actually available in this build environment; otherwise fall back to the two already-mandatory concurrency test tiers (backend HTTP CAS test, local coordinator-concurrency test) plus a two-simulator xcrun simctl push run that must be explicitly logged as simulated push delivery, never silently reported as satisfying the demo-critical R-007/R-011 requirements. Migration and seeding work is elevated to an explicit, first-class sub-deliverable of the schema milestone (M2): numbered idempotent SQL files plus an on-demand seed script producing two real accounts already joined to one real pod, ensuring the two-account verification protocol stays cheap to re-run rather than a manual chore skipped under time pressure. A new, separately timeboxed verification/repair milestone (M8) runs after the demo gate, specifically re-checking every core screen in both light and dark mode against Theme.swift for zero literal style values and zero placeholder/blank content, with fix time explicitly reserved, directly citing this fleet's own recorded design-lint and visual-QA incidents. The full milestone sequence (M0 stack/host/health, M1 contract freeze, M2 schema/migrations/seed, M3 CAS action endpoint with backend concurrency gate, M4 iOS domain/coordinator core with coordinator concurrency gate, M5 core UI build, M6 push/deep-link/offline hardening, M7 tiered verification demo, M8 dedicated repair pass) with named dependencies and exit gates is ready to hand off to task assignment.
open_risks: The exact hosting provider (Fly.io vs Railway vs Supabase-for-Postgres, etc.) is deferred to build-time discovery of what's actually usable in this workspace, and could still surface an unexpected capability gap if no externally-reachable hosting option exists here at all

The tiered APNs demo fallback depends on an honest, disciplined build agent actually labeling simulator-injected push as simulated rather than silently presenting it as a full pass — this has no automatic enforcement beyond being written down
The M8 repair pass depends on M0-M7 leaving enough schedule slack to actually execute it with real fix time, not just as a nominal final checkbox

All risks carried forward from every prior phase remain open: backend reachability is unproven until M0 actually executes, cold-start/network-density is unprovable in this build cycle, and CAS/APNs race-arbitration correctness must be demonstrated live across all three verification tiers, not just specified correctly on paper

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The task_assignments phase closed after two rounds with a fully reconciled, buildable backlog of 33 file-scoped tasks for pulse-relay, replacing an initial granularity mismatch (Codex's coarse 5-task milestone-level draft vs Claude's fine-grained 32-task draft) with a converged fine-grained backlog both participants endorsed. The four fixed lanes map directly onto the owning_lane tags tech_specs already assigned to every type and endpoint: data_domain owns migrations/seed plus Swift domain models and the pure reducer; services_utilities owns every backend route/service plus the API client, coordinator, keychain, and push/deep-link plumbing, and is responsible for the real deployed backend that M0's health-gate depends on; primary_ui owns the app shell, deep-link routing, and all eight screens; polish_resilience owns Theme.swift, the BeaconCard motion component, shared helpers, and the dark-mode/anti-literal repair pass, sequenced after every screen lands. The directory layout is locked as ios/PulseRelay/ (Xcode project/target named PulseRelay, correcting an App/App naming collision from one draft) and backend/ (Node+TypeScript). Branch and merge strategy is one branch and one PR per task (feature/<lane>/<task-id>-<slug>), squash-merged once each task's own dependencies and acceptance criteria are satisfied -- critically, the per-task dependency graph, not a blanket lane-sequential order, is the sole sequencing authority, since a hard lane-order would have contradicted the already-locked overlapping M3/M4/M5 milestone schedule from project_plan. Forbidden edit zones are locked per-lane with PulseRelayApp.swift and backend/src/server.ts as the only integrator-owned, announced-edit-only files. A previously-unowned task -- scaffolding the actual Xcode project itself (target, folder groups, Push Notifications and Sign in with Apple entitlements) -- was added as task T-033, a zero-dependency prerequisite for the first iOS file-creation tasks. Testing responsibility is split by lane, with the two hard CAS-correctness concurrency gates owned by services_utilities and the final honesty-checked three-tier verification report owned by polish_resilience. Requirement-ID coverage beyond the six IDs explicitly named in prior phases is flagged as an open item requiring reconciliation against the literal requirements.json before final build sign-off, rather than resolved with false precision.
open_risks: Requirement-ID coverage in the backlog beyond the six explicitly-named IDs is reconstructed best-effort, not verified against the literal requirements.json contract -- this must be reconciled before final build sign-off or some R-00x items could ship with no task actually naming them
The depends_on-graph-as-sole-authority sequencing model requires disciplined task-status tracking during build; if statuses aren't kept current, parallel lanes could still collide despite the plan
T-033's Xcode project scaffold has no fallback if project generation in this build environment hits unexpected tooling issues, since nothing downstream can proceed without it

All risks carried forward from every prior phase remain open: backend reachability is unproven until M0 actually executes, cold-start/network-density is unprovable in this build cycle, and CAS/APNs race-arbitration correctness must be demonstrated live across all three verification tiers, not just specified correctly on paper

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The implementation_readiness_gate phase closed after two rounds with a conditionally-ready verdict: the canonical 33-task backlog (T-001-T-033, ios/PulseRelay/ + backend/ Node+TS) is confirmed as final build scope across milestones M0-M8, no new features/screens added, and four concrete fixes were locked as edits to existing tasks/decisions rather than new blockers. First, the three contaminated tasks-json drafts left in task_assignments' session (React/Node-shaped paths, alternate R-0XX/T-0XX numbering) are explicitly declared void, with the 33-task list as the sole canonical backlog. Second, the long-deferred 'reconcile against requirements.json' obligation carried from app_features onward is retired: no such file was ever produced, and the operative acceptance contract is now frozen as the union of every task's own acceptance_criteria plus the six explicitly-named demo-critical items (R-006, R-007, R-009, R-010, R-011, R-037), against which T-032's verification report is graded. Third, an integrator-file ownership contradiction was found and fixed: PulseRelayApp.swift and backend/src/server.ts are limited to mount/register-only edits (announced before merge), while T-019's and T-006/T-010/T-012's real deliverables (AppGate/AppSession/AppRoute/DeepLinkRouter for primary_ui; routes/services for services_utilities) remain freely lane-owned. Fourth, pickup time was explicitly locked as implicit shared-pod context with no dedicated Request field in v1, consistent with the same-day-only/no-recurring boundary. Fifth, T-024 and T-032 gained explicit acceptance-criteria bullets for stale/expired deep-link handling (must render DeepLinkStateView, never a generic error) and force-quit-mid-accept reconciliation (must not duplicate actions or show false confidence), tightening existing tasks to match states already specified in design_handoff and ios_architecture_review without adding new task IDs. The gate closes with the build phase authorized to start immediately on T-033 (Xcode scaffold) and T-006 (backend skeleton + deploy) in parallel, per the existing zero-dependency task graph.
open_risks: The requirements-contract freeze (DEC-implementation_readiness_gate-003) depends on every future phase actually honoring it and not reintroducing a phantom requirements.json reconciliation obligation

The integrator-file split (DEC-implementation_readiness_gate-004) requires build-time discipline to keep composition-root edits truly minimal and announced, with no automatic enforcement beyond being written down

All risks carried forward from every prior phase remain open: backend reachability is unproven until M0 actually executes, cold-start/network-density is unprovable in this build cycle, and CAS/APNs race-arbitration correctness must be demonstrated live across all three verification tiers, not just specified correctly on paper

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This integration round confirmed rather than re-fixed the UI-crawl release-gate failure: all 17 declared-flow accessibility identifiers (authGate.signInWithAppleButton through requestDetail.viewReceiptButton, including the computed relayBoard.firstRequestCard) were independently verified present on real, correctly-gated, reachable controls across AuthGate, PodOnboarding, RelayBoard, RequestComposer, RequestDetail, and Receipt. The true root cause of the original gate failure -- AppSession.bootstrap() failing closed on every launch because no real backend host is deployed, which stranded the crawler at AuthGate regardless of downstream UI quality -- was already fixed in a prior round via a DEBUG-only CrawlModeHealthOverrideAPIClient in PulseRelayApp.swift gated on the -uiTestSeedSession launch argument, verified this round to be correctly scoped (Release builds untouched, only health() faked, all other API calls still hit the real placeholder host). The only new change this round was a minor design-lint fix: SettingsRow.swift's hardcoded .frame(width: 24) was replaced with a new DS.IconSize.settingsRowGlyph token in DesignSystem.swift. Two known issues were independently confirmed (not fixed, out of this change's scope): AppSession.requestId(from:) mis-parses pulserelay://request/<id> deep links since 'request' lands in the URL host rather than pathComponents, and the backend remains an undeployed placeholder host, meaning pod-creation and all other network calls still fail past the crawl-mode health bypass. The standing NO-GO launch verdict from final_review is unchanged by this round's work.
open_risks: The two-slash deep-link parsing bug in AppSession.requestId(from:) is confirmed real and still unfixed -- deep links from push notifications will silently fail to navigate to the target request until a future iteration fixes the URL-host-vs-pathComponents parsing logic.

Neither lane could actually run xcodebuild in this sandbox this round, so compile health after these two small file edits (DesignSystem.swift, SettingsRow.swift) is asserted from code review, not a verified build pass.

The backend remains an undeployed placeholder host (https://pulse-relay.invalid); the crawl-mode bypass only fakes health(), so no real end-to-end network flow (create pod, accept race, etc.) has ever executed against a live server -- the standing NO-GO verdict from final_review still applies regardless of this gate now passing.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This phase added a real, deterministic XCTest/Swift-Testing suite to the existing PulseRelayTests target: 64 test methods across 9 files (RequestSyncCoordinatorTests with 14 tests covering the accept-race winner/loser classification and force-quit recovery, CoordinatorRetryPolicyTests, AppSessionTests with 16 tests covering bootstrap/health-gate routing and deep-link parsing, DomainModelsTests, PushPayloadParserTests, AppErrorTests, ElapsedTimeFormattingTests, a shared TestFakes.swift support file with in-memory fakes for the API client/outbox/cache/keychain plus an EventCollector for draining the coordinator's AsyncStream, and the pre-existing ServiceUtilityTests.swift), all confirmed correctly registered in the pbxproj (each file has exactly 4 references matching the project's standard wiring pattern: file reference, build file, group entry, Sources build phase), with zero duplicate class names and zero network/timer dependencies. The integrator also removed a harmless but stray empty nested directory tree (ios/PulseRelay/ios/PulseRelay/Tests/..., zero files, confirmed before deletion) left over from a worker's path mistake, and independently verified two real, pre-existing production bugs the build lanes had found and correctly left undocumented-but-unfixed per this phase's rules rather than silently patching: RequestSyncCoordinator.queueOrFail's terminal-failure branch clears localOverrides keyed by the wrong dictionary key (clientActionId instead of requestId used everywhere else in the file), which can leave a request card stuck permanently in an awaiting-confirmation state after a legitimate server rejection -- a correctness bug in the exact state machine this app's core value proposition depends on; and AppSession.requestId(from:) only correctly parses the three-slash deep-link URL form, not the two-slash form its own doc comment claims to support, since 'request' lands in URL.host rather than .pathComponents for that format. Both are flagged as the top-priority fix for whichever phase next touches production code. SwiftUI view-body logic (inline submit() handlers in composer/pod-join views with no extracted view-model) was left deliberately untested per this phase's no-production-refactor rule, relying instead on the existing PulseRelayUITests happy-path test. No change was made to the app's functional status otherwise -- the backend remains undeployed, which is unrelated to this phase's scope but remains the dominant open risk for the app as a whole.
open_risks: RequestSyncCoordinator.queueOrFail clears localOverrides by the wrong key (clientActionId instead of requestId), which can leave a request card stuck in a false awaiting-confirmation state after a legitimate terminal rejection -- a real correctness bug in the core accept/release/withdraw state machine, found and documented via a test this phase but not fixed, since production-code changes are out of scope for write_tests

AppSession.requestId(from:) does not correctly parse the two-slash deep-link URL form its own doc comment claims to support (pulserelay://request/{id}), only the three-slash form -- found and the test was corrected to reflect real behavior rather than the documented-but-wrong format

The backend has still never been deployed to any real host across every build/verification round so far; the app's core value proposition (real-time, two-account, server-arbitrated accept race) has never executed end-to-end, and no test in this phase (by design, since tests must be deterministic and network-free) can substitute for that live proof

No compiler has been run in this environment at any point in this project's history; all wiring/correctness claims in this phase, like every phase before it, rest on manual pbxproj/text verification rather than a confirmed xcodebuild test run

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This phase produced the project's first real compiler-verified result: xcodebuild compiled the PulseRelay iOS app cleanly for the Simulator on attempt 0, after Claude (Codex was unavailable/CLI-skipped this round) independently re-read RequestSyncCoordinator.swift, confirmed the queueOrFail dictionary-key bug write_tests had found and left undocumented-but-unfixed was real, and repaired it with a minimal, non-feature change: queueOrFail now accepts an explicit requestId parameter and clears localOverrides under that key on terminal action failure, instead of the previously mismatched clientActionId key that silently no-op'd the removal and left request cards stuck showing false 'awaiting confirmation' state forever after a definitive server rejection (already-covered/forbidden/expired). The corresponding RequestSyncCoordinatorTests.swift test was rewritten from asserting the buggy stuck-state behavior to asserting the correct reverted-to-openUnclaimed behavior. The fix was verified by direct line-by-line diff review to be scoped exactly to the one affected call site (perform()), leaving the unrelated submit() call site's default nil-requestId no-op intact. The single most important unresolved fact carried forward from build_coordination and write_tests remains true and is not fixable by further code repair: the backend has never been deployed to any real, reachable host in this environment (backendBaseURL is still the deliberate .invalid placeholder, no deployment tooling exists in this sandbox, and outbound network calls are blocked), so the app's actual reason for existing -- a real-time, two-account, server-arbitrated accept race -- compiles and unit-tests cleanly but has never executed end-to-end against a live backend.
open_risks: The backend has never been deployed to any real, externally-reachable host in this build environment across every phase to date; the core two-device server-arbitrated accept-race proof required since prompt_contract (DEC-prompt_contract-008) remains completely unexecuted end-to-end, and this environment lacks the deployment tooling and network access to close that gap
Neither of the two mandated concurrency test tiers (backend HTTP CAS race test, local coordinator TaskGroup race test) has ever been written, only specified
Push notification dispatch remains a console.log placeholder, not real APNs integration

Sign-in-with-Apple backend verification derives a pseudo-identifier by hashing identityToken+nonce rather than validating Apple's identity token signature against Apple's public keys -- sufficient to prove the mechanism but not production-grade

This phase's compile-clean result covers build correctness only; it does not and cannot substitute for the live two-device/backend-reachability proof that remains the project's central unverified claim

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This phase produced a two-tier manual QA checklist for pulse-relay. Tier A covers everything actually runnable in this environment today with no backend: cold-launch/auth-failure honesty, offline queuing and the connection-banner two-copy-state rule, dark mode across all eight screens, full accessibility pass (VoiceOver sentence composition, 44x44 targets, Dynamic Type AX3-AX5, Reduce Motion crossfade, no color-only signaling), confirmation that zero paywall/StoreKit UI exists, force-quit persistence, and a regression check on the queueOrFail dictionary-key fix from build_verification. Tier B covers the actual point of the app -- pod onboarding empty states, join-code validation and revoke/reissue, no-child-PII posting, the non-optimistic awaiting-confirmation state, and above all the two-device accept race (exactly one latchedConfirmed and one latchedAlreadyCovered-by-name, run more than once to rule out a pass-by-luck result), force-quit-mid-accept reconciliation, release/withdraw mutual exclusivity, still-open aging/re-broadcast, receipt/audit correctness, and deep-link handling for withdrawn/expired requests -- all of which require a real deployed backend and two seeded accounts that do not yet exist in this build environment. The checklist explicitly calls out two previously-documented, still-real gaps (the two-slash deep-link parsing failure, and verifying the queueOrFail terminal-failure fix holds) as active items to check rather than silently assuming they're resolved. Codex was unavailable for this phase's only round; Claude's checklist was accepted as complete and honest without contradiction.
open_risks: Tier B of this checklist -- the entire core product proof (accept race, pod onboarding, receipts) -- remains completely unexecuted because no backend has ever been deployed to a reachable host in this environment

The two-slash deep-link parsing bug and the queueOrFail terminal-failure fix are both flagged for active verification in this checklist but have not actually been re-tested against a real compile/run since their respective discovery/fix phases

No concurrency test tier (backend HTTP CAS race, local coordinator TaskGroup race) has ever been written despite being mandated since ios_architecture_review, so Tier B item 6 (the accept race) has no automated backstop if the manual run is ever skipped under time pressure

All backend-reachability and cold-start/network-density risks carried forward from every prior phase remain open and unaddressed by this QA-checklist phase, which is documentation-only and cannot itself close them

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This phase produced App Store launch material for pulse-relay while explicitly refusing to call the app launch-ready. Positioning: app name 'Pulse Relay', subtitle 'Real-time pickup coverage for your school pod', category Lifestyle (not Social Networking) to avoid inviting UGC-moderation scrutiny the app doesn't structurally need. Three hard pre-submission blockers were named and distinguished from softer gaps: the backend has never been deployed (backendBaseURL still .invalid, guaranteeing a Guideline 2.1 rejection since every reviewer hits a stuck AuthGate), the test target currently fails to compile (duplicate PushPayloadError declaration, confirmed by the latest xcodebuild run), and no Privacy Policy or Support URL exists anywhere since nothing is hosted -- App Store Connect hard-blocks submission without both. A single judgment-call review risk was identified as more dangerous than the mechanical blockers: Guideline 1.2 (UGC) normally expects reporting/blocking/moderation, which this app deliberately ships without; the mitigation is App Review notes that preemptively frame the app as a closed trust-graph pod (people who already know each other) rather than an open social feed, not building moderation now. The privacy nutrition label was characterized as genuinely clean -- no location, contacts, photos, or child PII, only first-party Apple-identifier-derived account ID, pod membership, and request/action records, zero tracking/IDFA/ad SDKs -- a real differentiator for a parent audience. Permission copy is locked to exactly two prompts (system Sign in with Apple, and remote notifications requested post-pod-onboarding with a specific rationale line). Subscription/paywall review risk is effectively zero since no StoreKit or IAP exists in the shipped build, but marketing copy was explicitly barred from describing the deferred three-unlock subscription plan from per_app_product_brief since describing unshipped features risks a 2.3.1 rejection. A four-screenshot plan was locked (pulsing open board, confirmed/latched board, pod join screen, receipt/share card) with no App Preview video for v1, since a scripted video would undersell an interaction whose value depends on real use. The phase closed by distinguishing two different bars explicitly: 'passes App Review' (achievable once the three hard blockers close) versus 'safe to actually launch to parents coordinating real pickups' (which also needs real APNs integration and genuine Sign-in-with-Apple signature verification, neither of which a reviewer will catch but both of which matter for real trust).
open_risks: The backend has still never been deployed to any reachable host across every phase in this project's history; until it is, the app cannot pass App Review at all, regardless of how complete the launch material is
The test target's compile error (duplicate PushPayloadError) is a same-day fix but remains unresolved as of this phase's verification snapshot
No Privacy Policy or Support URL exists yet since nothing is hosted -- this is a distinct, independent blocker from backend deployment and must not be assumed to resolve itself alongside it

The Guideline 1.2 UGC framing defense is a reviewer judgment call, not a guarantee -- if a reviewer disagrees with the closed-pod characterization, rejection risk remains even with the explanatory App Review notes

Real APNs integration and genuine Sign-in-with-Apple signature validation remain unresolved; neither blocks App Review submission but both matter for whether the app is actually trustworthy for real families in a real emergency

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This review evaluated the just-completed UI-crawl release-gate fix (a DEBUG-only CrawlModeHealthOverrideAPIClient bypass in PulseRelayApp.swift, gated on -uiTestSeedSession, that fakes a healthy backend response for crawl sessions) and confirmed it was correctly and narrowly scoped: all 17 declared-flow accessibility identifiers were already present on real controls, the bypass touches only DEBUG/crawl-mode sessions and leaves Release builds and every other API call (createPod, joinPod, etc.) hitting the real placeholder backend host unchanged, and the build verifies cleanly via xcodebuild. The review's core finding is that this fix changes the crawler's experience, not a real user's: a real device on a real launch still calls the real (unreachable) https://pulse-relay.invalid host and fails closed at AppSession.bootstrap() exactly as before, so the gate now passing must not be read as the app working end-to-end. The standing launch verdict is therefore explicitly reaffirmed unchanged -- NO-GO for launch/App Store submission, GO to continue building -- and the review flags that backend deployment has now been named the single highest-leverage next action across four consecutive phases (final_review, iterate_scope, build_coordination, this round) without anyone actually doing it, elevating this from a technical gap to a process risk needing explicit ownership. The confirmed, still-unfixed two-slash deep-link parsing bug in AppSession.requestId(from:) is restated as an independent, cheap, launch-blocking fix that should not lose priority. The idea itself (pod-scoped pickup coverage, accept-race CAS mechanic) continues to be judged as a strong, complete answer to the original creative/architectural brief; only the 'actually working end-to-end against a live backend' clause remains unmet.
open_risks: Backend remains undeployed; no accept-race, pod-creation, or other network flow has ever executed against a live server, and the mandated concurrency tests and two-device demo cannot meaningfully run until it is.
The two-slash deep-link parsing bug in AppSession.requestId(from:) remains real and unfixed across multiple rounds now -- push-driven deep links silently fail to navigate.

The 'deploy the backend' recommendation has now recurred across four phases without execution -- a process/ownership gap, not just a remaining technical task, that risks the project cycling indefinitely on narrow, well-scoped-but-non-load-bearing fixes.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The portfolio_audit phase confirmed, with Claude solo (Codex unavailable) and no substantive disagreement possible on a structural check, that pulse-relay's portfolio shape is not applicable in the multi-app sense: this has been a locked single-app build since portfolio_selection (DEC-portfolio_selection-001), with exactly one expected and one actual project (ios/PulseRelay/ Xcode project plus backend/ Node+TypeScript service) under one root, no child app folders, no portfolio_json manifest introduced at any point across task_assignments/implementation_readiness_gate/build_coordination/all verification phases, and therefore no categories were ever split out and none could have been silently collapsed. The phase explicitly flagged one honesty limit: the confirmation rests on the internally-consistent decisions log and phase transcripts, not a fresh filesystem crawl of the real build tree (pulse-relay/app_build/), which this sandbox cannot access -- so a stray artifact dropped by some build lane can't be ruled out by disk inspection here, only by the absence of any such artifact ever being mentioned across 20+ phases of documentation. Backfill guidance for Jira/Notion was given as one single epic for pulse-relay (no child epics) with the eight ordered follow-up items from final_review as its ticket list in the same priority order. The phase was explicitly scoped as a structural confirmation stamp only, not a reopening of the final_review/app_store_readiness NO-GO-for-launch verdict or its follow-up ordering, both of which remain authoritative as written.
open_risks: This audit could not independently verify via filesystem access that no stray second project, sibling app folder, or accidental portfolio_json file exists in the real build tree -- it relies entirely on the absence of any such artifact being mentioned across the full decision/phase-summary record

All substantive risks carried forward from final_review and app_store_readiness remain fully open and untouched by this phase: the backend has never been deployed to any reachable host, the test target still fails to compile on the twice-flagged duplicate PushPayloadError bug, neither mandated concurrency test has been written, the two-device accept-race demo has never run, and the app remains NO-GO for launch/App Store submission pending the ordered eight-item follow-up list

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This phase scoped the fix for the failing release gate (UI crawl couldn't find podOnboarding.createPodButton and reported '+7 more' missing controls, with only authGate.signInWithAppleButton actually reachable). The diagnosis: this is almost certainly an accessibility-identifier wiring gap, not a missing feature — PodOnboarding's create-pod path was already built per the locked screen graph, but identifiers appear to have been wired only for AuthGate and never carried into downstream post-auth screens. The committed scope is a bounded instrumentation sweep across every screen named in docs/ui_crawl.json's declared flows: add correct accessibilityIdentifier values to existing controls, and only where a control is genuinely absent, add the minimal SwiftUI affordance using existing Theme tokens with no new navigation or business logic. Changes are confined to SwiftUI view files under Features/; RequestSyncCoordinator, the reducer, Network/State internals, backend routes, and the integrator-owned composition-root files remain untouched. This sandbox has no filesystem access to the actual app_build tree (consistent with the prior portfolio_audit phase's finding), so this scope was set from the decisions log and gate message rather than a direct diff against PodOnboarding's view code — the next phase with real file access must open docs/ui_crawl/'s failing screenshot first to confirm the diagnosis before editing.
open_risks: The diagnosis (missing identifiers vs. a genuinely unbuilt affordance) is inferred from the decisions log and gate message text, not from actually opening docs/ui_crawl/'s screenshot or PodOnboarding's view code — if PodOnboarding's create-pod path is truly absent from the build, this is a bigger fix than instrumentation and the scope in this decision would need to be revisited.

The '+7 more' controls named by the gate are not individually enumerated here; whoever builds this must pull the full list from docs/ui_crawl.json rather than assuming the fix ends at the one named createPodButton.
